messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Arjun, a 29-year-old painter from a South Asian background, found himself ensnared in a web of anxiety and fear following a traumatic mugging last year. The incident had left an indelible mark on him. He vividly recalled the evening when he was walking home from a late job, paintbrushes still tucked under his arm, when a group of men confronted him. The memory of that confrontation loomed heavily in his mind, making every shadow and every unfamiliar figure on the street feel like an imminent threat, as if danger could strike again at any moment. He remembered the rush of adrenaline, the fear coursing through his veins as they demanded his wallet and phone. The ordeal lasted mere minutes, but it felt like an eternity, and he would wake up in a cold sweat, haunted by nightmares of the event—dreams where he relived the moment again and again, the panic rising in his chest as he struggled to break free. Each time he awoke, he felt a surge of irritability, an angry outburst bubbling just beneath the surface. It was as if he had become a stranger to himself, his body always on high alert, constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats. 

The physical locations where the mugging had occurred became charged with anxiety. The memories flooding back in those places carried a palpable sense of danger, as if the threat he had once faced was still lurking just out of sight, making each return feel like an invitation to experience fear anew. Each time he encountered these reminders of his trauma, he found himself thinking that this was what his life had become — an endless cycle of fear and vulnerability that he could never escape. Simply passing by those streets triggered a rush of intrusive memories, causing his heart to race and his palms to sweat. These memories flooded back with such intensity that they felt alive, forcing him to relive the fear and vulnerability of the event as if it were happening anew, amplifying his sense of threat. These moments magnified the tense state his body had adopted; he felt as if he were perpetually ready to react to danger, a sensation that transformed his daily life into a battleground. The memories that surfaced in those moments only served to heighten his sense of danger, making him feel as though he was back in the confrontation, every detail sharp and close, reinforcing his belief that he was under constant threat. The world outside was a constant reminder of his trauma, and each spatial trigger intensified his belief that he could no longer trust the people around him. Each time he encountered these triggers, his body would react with a surge of fear, amplifying the sense of threat that loomed over him, as if danger was not just a memory but a present reality. He had come to mistrust everyone, convinced that anyone could become a threat, and this growing isolation made him feel more detached from those he loved. His certainty that he was always at risk led him to interpret even innocent interactions as potential betrayals, reinforcing the belief that he could not trust anyone. This deep-seated belief that he was always vulnerable led him to interpret every interaction with others as a potential source of danger, making him more anxious and guarded in social situations. His negative beliefs about his own safety shaped how he viewed the world, instilling a persistent sense of danger that made him hyper-aware of any situation where he might feel exposed or vulnerable. Having come to believe that he was always at risk, Arjun approached even the most mundane interactions with an underlying tension, bracing himself for potential threats that existed only in his mind. 

As he grappled with these feelings, Arjun found it difficult to piece together the memory of the mugging. Yet, whenever those fragmented memories surfaced, they were accompanied by a crushing sense of immediacy, leading him to feel as if the danger of that night was still very much alive, echoing within him. Every time those memories broke through, he couldn’t shake the thought that if he kept reliving the trauma, it only confirmed his fear that he was weak and unworthy of safety. He often felt as though he was only recalling fragments of the experience, the gaps gnawing at him and fueling his guilt. Each time those fragments emerged, he couldn't help but think they revealed a deep flaw within himself, reinforcing his belief that he was weak and unworthy of safety, which further fueled his anxiety about future threats. Once those memories broke through, they amplified his sense of danger, as if the past were still alive within him, creating an ever-present anxiety that made it hard to feel secure anywhere. Each time those fragments surfaced, they deepened his conviction that he had failed to protect himself, reinforcing his belief that he was inadequate and leaving him feeling hopeless and trapped. He would sit in his studio, attempting to deliberate on the event, but the harder he tried to access the painful recollections, the more elusive they became. This incomplete picture of the traumatic event compounded his feelings of guilt; he often questioned why he hadn’t fought back or run faster, which only deepened his sense of inadequacy. The memories, though fragmented, remained potent triggers—each recall would send him spiraling back into that moment of vulnerability, enhancing his sense of danger and leading him to believe that he was incapable of relying on anyone, not even himself.

Arjun's negative appraisals shaped his perception of the world, creating a vicious cycle. His mistrust of people steered him towards isolation, which only fortified his belief that he couldn’t rely on others. As he withdrew from social interactions, he would find himself alone in his thoughts, the memories of the mugging replaying in his mind, reinforcing his feelings of vulnerability. The threat he felt was not just from the memories themselves; it seeped into every aspect of his life, making even casual encounters feel like potential ambushes, further pushing him into isolation. This heightened sense of threat made him hyper-vigilant, as he began to perceive danger in ordinary situations, each unexpected sound or glance confirming his belief that he was constantly in peril. This constant reflection contributed to his irritability and made him more sensitive to perceived slights from others, aggravating his readiness to react defensively. With an ever-present sense of threat, even minor interactions felt charged; he interpreted casual remarks as veiled attacks, convinced that others were judging him, and this only solidified his desire to withdraw further into isolation. His memories of the traumatic event seemed to taunt him, leading him to interpret innocent interactions as threats, convinced that others were judging him or harboring malicious intent. Each day became a struggle as he navigated through the layers of his trauma, caught in an ever-tightening loop of anxiety and avoidance.

When Arjun finally sought help, he felt a glimmer of hope mixed with the fear of confronting his trauma. He was acutely aware that the memories he carried would not only resurface but could also amplify his fears, making every session feel like stepping into a minefield of emotions he had long tried to avoid. He harbored a deep-seated worry that delving into his memories would only serve to amplify his feelings of guilt and mistrust, but he knew he could not continue living in this state of hypervigilance. He longed to reclaim the joy he once found in painting, to reconnect with his wife and friends without the shadow of his trauma looming overhead. Yet, he feared that engaging with those memories would only serve to reinforce his belief that he was permanently broken, trapped in a cycle of pain and mistrust that he couldn't escape. With each session, he hoped to find a way to unravel the knots of his experience, to understand the connection between the past and present, and to ultimately heal from the scars that had come to define his daily existence.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: The vignette does not convey how triggers lead to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette does not convey how negative appraisals lead to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not convey how memory influences negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Threat: The vignette does not convey how memory influences a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The memories flooding back in those places carried a palpable sense of danger, as if the threat he had once faced was still lurking just out of sight, making each return feel like an invitation to experience fear anew. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each encounter with these reminders intensified the feeling of danger, causing Arjun's heartbeat to quicken and his breath to shorten, as if the threat of the mugging was reawakening within him, ready to strike again. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
His certainty that he was always at risk led him to interpret even innocent interactions as potential betrayals, reinforcing the belief that he could not trust anyone. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This belief that he was a target, not just unlucky, but chosen, made every new situation feel like a test he was destined to fail, amplifying the sense of threat that permeated his daily life. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Yet, whenever those fragmented memories surfaced, they were accompanied by a crushing sense of immediacy, leading him to feel as if the danger of that night was still very much alive, echoing within him. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After those memories broke through, Arjun would find himself grappling with the thought that if he kept reliving the trauma, it confirmed a deeper flaw within himself, reinforcing his negative self-appraisals and enhancing the threat he felt from the world around him. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Once those memories broke through, they amplified his sense of danger, as if the past were still alive within him, creating an ever-present anxiety that made it hard to feel secure anywhere. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The flashbacks left him feeling hunted in his own home, as though the danger had not receded into memory but had instead taken up residence within him, ready to pounce at any moment. 
<<<END>>>
